idiom_name: token rule table (null/left-denotation handlers) + binding-power loop
implementation_notes: Give every token type a rule: a prefix handler for tokens that can start an expression, an infix/postfix handler for tokens that extend one, and a numeric binding power that orders them against each other. The parser reads a token, invokes its prefix handler to build a left expression, then loops while the lookahead token's binding power is at least the caller's minimum, consuming the operator and letting its left handler absorb the expression parsed so far. Right-associative operators recurse with their own binding power, left-associative ones with one more, and prefix operators pick a power just above the constructs they should absorb. Keep the rules in one table so the grammar stays data, add a nesting-depth guard before the host stack limit is reached, and keep lexing, dispatch and semantic action separate. When the grammar grows beyond expressions, hand the precedence over to a parser generator instead of extending the table indefinitely.
code_sketch:
rules[token.type] = { nud, led, lbp }

expr(min_bp):
    tok  = next()
    left = rules[tok.type].nud(tok)              # prefix / primary
    while min_bp < rules[peek().type].lbp:       # infix / postfix
        op   = next()
        left = rules[op.type].led(left, op)      # led recurses with its own
    return left                                  # or with lbp + 1 (left-assoc)
pitfalls: Encoding the grammar in control flow again - an if/else chain over operator spellings inside the loop - so that every new operator edits the core algorithm instead of adding a row.
Choosing binding powers and recursion offsets independently per operator until associativity is no longer derivable from the table.
Treating the parser stack as unbounded: without a depth guard, nested input turns a syntax error into a crash.

Wrong move: let plugins register operators without validating tokenization and precedence -> distinct spellings can collide or associate unexpectedly -> instead validate operator tokens, binding powers and associativity at registration and test cross-operator pairs.
